To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
local compliance is low and community-supported enforcement has the potential to increase local compliance rates in the region.

local compliance with marine resource rules is low and that community-supported enforcement is a promising approach for increasing compliance and enforcement in the Coral Triangle, especially when it is supported by local capacity development.
local enforcement is the most important determinant of compliance with marine resource management rules and regulations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the need for capacity-building and institutional strengthening of local compliance and community-supported enforcement efforts.

the need for a shift from a compliance and enforcement model that relies on coercive measures to a model that emphasizes the development of local support for enforcement and the use of non-coercive mechanisms to increase local compliance.
identifying the capacity needs of local compliance and community-supported enforcement of marine resource rules and regulation and the priority of these needs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a strong need to build local capacity for compliance and enforcement, but this must be a long-term investment and not a one-time event.

there is a need to develop a comprehensive, multi-faceted, multi-level, and multi-stakeholder strategy to address the complex and multi-dimensional challenges of compliance and enforcement in the Coral Triangle.

local capacity to support enforcement efforts is a key factor in increasing compliance and enforcement of marine resource rules and regulation and that this capacity can be built over time with appropriate investment and training.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the capacity for local compliance and enforcement is low, the capacity to support enforcement efforts is low and the priority for capacity development is high.
local compliance and enforcement efforts are not only possible but also highly effective and sustainable.
the capacity to enforce marine resource rules and regulation in the Coral Triangle has not kept pace with the need for enforcement.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is a clear need for a more comprehensive understanding of the role and potential contribution of local compliance and community-supported enforcement to the management and conservation of fisheries and marine protected areas.

the most effective compliance and enforcement systems are those that are perceived by local fishers to be legitimate, fair and accountable and are supported by a personal morality and social environment that supports and reinforces compliance.
the most effective enforcement is not necessarily the most visible enforcement.
